faq.q: Can stress be good for you?
faq.a: Yes, a little. Short, manageable stress makes you alert and focused, so you can do your best in a test, a match or a show. It is too much stress, for too long, that causes problems.

faq.q: How do I know if I am too stressed?
faq.a: Signs include trouble sleeping, headaches or tummy aches, snapping at people, finding it hard to focus, or feeling like crying a lot, especially if it lasts for weeks.
asks: How much stress is too much?

faq.q: What can I do if I feel too stressed?
faq.a: Break tasks into small steps, take regular breaks, move your body, sleep well and talk to someone. A trusted grown-up, a school counsellor or a doctor can also help.
asks: How do I get less stressed?

faq.q: Why do I freeze in exams?
faq.a: When stress is very high, your brain's alarm takes over and the thinking part goes quiet, so your mind can feel blank. Slow breathing for a minute can help it switch back on.
asks: Why does my mind go blank in tests?

faq.q: Is the stress curve the same for everyone?
faq.a: No. People and tasks are different. Hard, new tasks are usually done best with less stress, while simple tasks can handle a bit more.
asks: Do some people handle stress better?

facts: The stress curve is known as the Yerkes-Dodson law, after psychologists Robert Yerkes and John Dodson, who published their experiment in 1908.
Their research suggested that harder tasks are done best with less stress than simple tasks.
